sections.section_title: Initial Presentation: Sepsis and the Role of Capnocytophaga canimorsus
sections.description: This section covers the early clinical presentation of the patient, the nature of the causative pathogen, and the immediate management of septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
subtopics: Clinical presentation of C. canimorsus infection: from dog bites to fulminant sepsis
Microbiology of Capnocytophaga canimorsus: fastidious growth and diagnostic challenges
Recognizing septic shock and multiorgan failure in the zoonotic context
The intersection of sepsis and DIC: pancytopenia, coagulopathy, and acute kidney injury (AKI)
Initial empiric antibiotic selection for dog-associated pathogens

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology: From Infectious Trigger to Complement Dysregulation
sections.description: This section explains the biological mechanisms that link a bacterial infection to the development of a thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), specifically focusing on the alternative complement pathway.
subtopics: Overview of the alternative complement pathway and its regulatory proteins (Factors H, I, and B)
Complement-mediated haemolytic uraemic syndrome (CM-HUS) in immunocompetent adults
The 'second hit' hypothesis: how infection triggers TMA in predisposed or susceptible hosts
Complement susceptibility of C. canimorsus and its role in endothelial damage
The paradoxical role of complement: host defense vs. uncontrolled activation

sections.section_title: The Diagnostic Shift: Distinguishing DIC from TMA
sections.description: This section focuses on the critical clinical transition where the patient's condition evolved from sepsis-related DIC to a distinct thrombotic microangiopathy, detailing the diagnostic markers used to identify this shift.
subtopics: Clinical red flags for TMA: isolated drop in hemoglobin and persistent thrombocytopenia post-sepsis
Laboratory markers of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA): LDH, haptoglobin, and schistocytes
Differentiating DIC and TMA: timing of onset and laboratory trends
Interpreting the Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT) and pitfalls of false positives in the context of penicillin/transfusions
The role of the peripheral blood smear in identifying schistocytes

sections.description: This section outlines the logical process of ruling out other forms of TMA to arrive at a diagnosis of CM-HUS, including the use of specialized tests and histology.
subtopics: Ruling out Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP): the role of ADAMTS13 activity and PLASMIC score
Excluding Shiga toxin-producing E. coli-associated HUS (STEC-HUS) via stool PCR
The role of renal biopsy: identifying fibrin thrombi and acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
Interpreting complement studies: why normal C3/C4 levels do not exclude CM-HUS
Functional assays and extended genetic testing for hereditary complement defects

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Management: Complement Blockade and Risk Mitigation
sections.description: This section discusses the treatment strategies employed, the differences between plasma exchange and monoclonal antibodies, and the specific safety concerns regarding eculizumab.
subtopics: Mechanism of action of Eculizumab: targeting terminal complement component C5
Plasma Exchange (PEX) as bridging therapy: benefits and limitations in CM-HUS
The therapeutic dilemma: using complement inhibitors during active bacteraemia
Preventing eculizumab-associated infections: meningococcal vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics
Impact of treatment timing on renal recovery and long-term prognosis

sections.description: The final section evaluates the patient's recovery and summarizes the key educational takeaways for clinicians managing complex TMAs triggered by infection.
subtopics: Evaluating renal recovery: interpreting serum creatinine and diuresis post-treatment
Maintenance therapy and criteria for the discontinuation of eculizumab
The significance of infection-triggered CM-HUS in the absence of genetic mutations
Key takeaways for early recognition of TMA in septic patients
The necessity of integrated multidisciplinary care (Infectious Disease, Nephrology, and Haematology)
